t: Domain Classification Engine: a plain-language overview
title: Domain Classification Engine: a plain-language overview
description: Overview: what the Domain Classification Engine does and why archives need it. A domain classification engine reads a record and decides which field it belongs to: medicine, engineering, law, astronomy, cooking, and so on. It learns the vocabulary of each field — 'telescope' smells like astronomy, 'tort' smells like law — and scores every record against every field. Each record lands in its right department.
provenance: Public methods compiled from standard information-extraction and knowledge-organization practice. Assembled for the JAH Databases archive.

t: How the Domain Classification Engine works
title: How the Domain Classification Engine works
description: Overview: what the Domain Classification Engine does and why archives need it. Real classifiers score documents against domain gazetteers (curated keyword lists per field) or train models like multinomial naive Bayes and linear SVMs on labeled corpora; modern systems fine-tune transformer models for the same task. Hierarchical classification first picks a broad area (science) then a specialty (astrophysics), and multi-label mode allows a bioinformatics paper to carry both biology and computing. Each assignment carries a confidence score, and low-confidence records go to human review.
provenance: Public methods compiled from standard information-extraction and knowledge-organization practice. Assembled for the JAH Databases archive.

t: How the Domain Classification Engine works: the deep tour
title: How the Domain Classification Engine works: the deep tour
description: Overview: what the Domain Classification Engine does and why archives need it. Real classifiers score documents against domain gazetteers (curated keyword lists per field) or train models like multinomial naive Bayes and linear SVMs on labeled corpora; modern systems fine-tune transformer models for the same task. Hierarchical classification first picks a broad area (science) then a specialty (astrophysics), and multi-label mode allows a bioinformatics paper to carry both biology and computing. Each assignment carries a confidence score, and low-confidence records go to human review. Advanced engines calibrate their confidence scores so '90%' means 90% right, detect out-of-domain records that match nothing, and adapt to vocabulary drift as fields evolve. Quality is measured by macro-F1 across domains on held-out labeled sets. The limits are genuinely interdisciplinary works and emerging fields with no training data — those get multi-label assignments with modest confidence rather than a forced single label, because a wrong department is worse than an honest 'several'.
provenance: Public methods compiled from standard information-extraction and knowledge-organization practice. Assembled for the JAH Databases archive.
